title: Mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics in a mobile oware game
instructions:
## A studio in Accra is building mobile oware

You join the design team for a phone version of oware (abapa rules). Use the MDA framework to read the game: **mechanics** are the rules and actions, **dynamics** are the behaviour that emerges when people play them, and **aesthetics** are the feelings players have. Then use playtest data to fix a balance problem.

nodes.title: A rule
nodes.text: Read the rules sheet. Which MDA layer is "sow seeds one per house anticlockwise; capture when the last seed makes a house of 2 or 3"?

evidence.title: Rules sheet (abapa)
evidence.text: Two rows of six houses, four seeds each. On your turn pick up all seeds from one of your houses and sow them one per house anticlockwise. If the last seed lands in an opponent's house making 2 or 3, capture them, and keep capturing backwards while the previous house also has 2 or 3. You may not leave your opponent with no seeds if you can avoid it. First to 25 seeds wins.

choices.feedback: Correct. It is a rule that defines an action and its result.
Dynamics are what happens when players use the rules, not the rules themselves.
Aesthetics are player feelings, not rules.

nodes.title: A behaviour
nodes.text: Experienced players let seeds pile up in one house (a "kroo") to sow round the whole board later for a large capture. Nothing in the rules tells them to. Which layer?

choices.text: A dynamic: strategy that emerges from the mechanics in play
choices.feedback: Correct. Designers cannot write dynamics directly. They emerge from the mechanics.
It is a behaviour. The feeling it produces is the aesthetic.

nodes.title: A feeling
nodes.text: Testers say the best moment is "when you are far behind and one big sow turns it around". Which of the eight kinds of fun is this mainly?

choices.text: Challenge: the tension of overcoming an obstacle through skill
choices.feedback: Correct. A comeback earned by planning is challenge, with some drama on top.

nodes.title: A balance problem
nodes.text: Look at the playtest data. What is happening and what should you change?

evidence.title: Playtest data, 200 games against the AI
evidence.text:
Player who captures first wins: 86% of games.
Average seeds behind when a comeback happened: 3.
Comebacks from 8 or more seeds behind: 2 of 200 games.
Median game length: 9 minutes; 41% of losing players quit before the end.

choices.text: A positive feedback loop: the leader gets more seeds and more options. Add a negative feedback rule, such as a hint or bonus move for the trailing player in single-player mode
choices.feedback: Correct. Positive feedback snowballs a lead. Negative feedback keeps the outcome uncertain, which is what makes players stay.
That makes the snowball faster, not slower.
Length is not the cause. The early lead is.

nodes.title: Two perspectives
nodes.text: Why does MDA matter when you change a rule?

choices.text: Designers change mechanics, but players meet the aesthetics first, so every rule change must be judged by how it changes dynamics and feelings in play
choices.feedback: Correct. That is why the next step is another playtest, not a release.

choices.text: Players care most about the rules
choices.feedback: Players experience feelings. Most never read the rules.

choices.text: Aesthetics can be added after the rules are final
choices.feedback: Aesthetics come from the mechanics and dynamics. They cannot be bolted on.

nodes.title: Design note written
nodes.text: You document the snowball problem and propose a catch-up mechanic for single-player mode, to be measured in the next playtest by comeback rate and quit rate.

hints: Mechanics are written down. Dynamics emerge in play. Aesthetics are felt.
When the leader keeps getting stronger, that is positive feedback.
Judge a rule change by what players do and feel afterwards.

checks.label: You read the rules and the playtest data
At least four of the five decisions are right
checks.message: Fewer than four of the five were right. Read the feedback and run the case again.

realityNote: Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek introduced MDA in 2004. Studios still use comeback rate and early-quit rate to find snowballing in competitive games.
